study_identification.title: Delineating the Heterogeneity of Alzheimer ' s Disease and Mild Cognitive Impairment Using Normative Models of Dynamic Brain Functional Networks

study_characteristics.study_objective: To delineate the heterogeneity of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and identify subtypes based on deviations from normative models of dynamic brain functional networks.

dataset_name.reason: The paper clearly states the datasets used. Dataset 1 is Cam-CAN, Dataset 2 is MCAD (Multicenter Alzheimer Disease Imaging Consortium), and Dataset 3 is ADNI.
dataset_name.supporting_text: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans of 1896 individuals were acquired from 3 datasets. Dataset 1, which included 644 healthy individuals, was used in this work to build a normative model and was obtained from the Cambridge Centre for Aging and Neuroscience repository (Cam-CAN, available at http://www.mrc-cbu.cam.ac.uk/datasets/camcan/) (24,25). Dataset 2 comprised 257 normal control (NC) participants, 257 patients with MCI, and 295patients with AD from the MCAD (Multicenter Alzheimer Disease Imaging Consortium) dataset. Dataset 3 included 259 NC participants and 184 patients with MCI from the ADNI (Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative) database (https://adni.loni.usc.edu/), which was used to investigate longitudinal changes in MCI.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: To investigate the deviation patterns in subtypes of AD and MCI, we calculated the average deviation of each subgroup and assessed the similarity between AD and MCI subtypes using Spearman correlations. We compared the differences between subtypes in clinical characteristics (using the MiniMental State Examination [MMSE] for all individuals, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment [MoCA] scores available from 5 sites) with age and sex as covariates. Furthermore, differences in deviation patterns, functional connections, and structural features were identi /uniFB01 ed using 2-sample t tests with age, sex, and head motion as covariates. Multiple comparisons were corrected using the false discovery rate method (corrected a = .05). We replicated the experiment on dataset 3 to investigate the robustness of our /uniFB01 ndings. We used Kaplan-Meier survival analysis to assess the risk of MCI subtypes progressing to AD. The logarithmic rank test (36) evaluated differences in survival rates among MCI subgroups, with survival rates indicating MCI diagnosis maintenance. A linear regression model was used to estimate cognitive decline duration in subtypes over time, with age and sex as covariates.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: The study identified two distinct subtypes of AD and MCI with different brain functional phenotypes, spatial atrophy patterns, disease progression, and cognitive decline trajectories.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Two subtypes were identified for both AD and MCI (AD-1/AD-2, MCI-1/MCI-2). AD-1 and MCI-1 showed positive deviation patterns, while AD-2 and MCI-2 showed negative deviation patterns. The subtypes with positive deviations in AD and MCI shared similar patterns, as did those with negative deviations. MCI-2 showed a higher conversion rate to AD and a more rapid cognitive decline. The subtypes also differed in functional connectivity and structural features (GMV and cortical thickness).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Several limitations of the current study should be considered. First, scanning protocols varied across datasets and sites. To mitigate site effects on the calculation of deviations, we computed the mean deviation of the NC participants as a baseline for each site to adjust the deviations for patients accordingly. Second, longitudinal data were unavailable in the in-house dataset, so we used the participants with MCI from ADNI as an independent site for validation. We also noted that the sample size of the MCI group with longitudinal data is relatively small, which cautions us to interpret some of the results carefully. Finally, various neuropathological patterns identi /uniFB01 ed across different imaging modalities may give rise to distinct subtypes. The extent to which the subtyping /uniFB01 ndings derived from other features/modalities correspond to overlapping patient subgroups remains unclear, presenting a challenging area of research (42,58 -60). Further studies that incorporate more factors would be important for exploring the causes of subtype emergence.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The use of dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) patterns to investigate neurobiological heterogeneity is a key innovation. The study also uses a normative modeling approach to quantify individual deviations from a healthy baseline.
